title: Linear Algebra
summary: Linear algebra in R^n for first-year computer scientists, following Lay's Linear Algebra and Its Applications: linear systems and row reduction, matrix algebra, subspaces, determinants, eigenvalues, orthogonality and least squares. Twenty lectures come with pre-lecture videos and Grasple exercises, plus weekly construction blocks and an instruction session. Two lectures train academic reasoning: proving a true statement or refuting a false one with an explicit counterexample.

basis.description: The CSE1205 lecture slides (Lectures 1 to 20 as text; Lecture 21, exam training, left out), the official CSE1205 description and the 2022 to 2024 papers. Time shares count content slides; the general proof-method slides of Lectures 7 and 17 are left out and their worked statements counted under the topic they treat.
basis.caveat: From 2026-27 the course is CSE13A, renamed from CSE1205 with content unchanged, still in year 1, quarter 3. The official description weighs the midterm at 20 percent, the Lecture 1 slides at 25 percent: check the current rule. LU decomposition is in the official description but not in the slides. Slide counts understate determinants (a full lecture on only 12 slides).

topics.name: Linear systems, spans and linear independence
lectures: Lecture 1 - Linear systems and echelon forms-course organization
Lecture 3 - Solution sets and linear independence
know: Elementary row operations, echelon and reduced echelon form, pivot positions, basic and free variables
A system has no, exactly one or infinitely many solutions; it is inconsistent exactly when an echelon form of the augmented matrix has a row 0 ... 0 | b with b not 0
The three equivalent forms of one problem: a system of equations, a vector equation x1 a1 + ... + xn an = b, and a matrix equation Ax = b
Span and its picture in R^2 and R^3 (a line or plane through the origin); Ax = b is solvable for every b exactly when A has a pivot in every row
Ax = 0 is always consistent; its solutions in parametric vector form; the solutions of Ax = b are one particular solution plus all solutions of Ax = 0
Linear independence: x1 v1 + ... + xp vp = 0 has only the trivial solution; shortcuts: more vectors than entries, or a set containing 0, is always dependent
do: Find the values of a parameter h for which a system is inconsistent, has one solution or has infinitely many
Write the general solution in parametric vector form from a reduced echelon form
Decide whether a vector lies in a span, or find where lines given in parametric form meet
Test a set of vectors with a parameter in it for linear independence
Prove that vectors built from an independent set, such as v1 - v2, v2 and v2 - v3, are independent again
pitfalls: Dividing by an expression containing the parameter during row reduction without checking the values that make it zero: the 2023 endterm question had three bad values of h, one of them hidden this way
Concluding infinitely many solutions from a free variable without first checking that the system is consistent

topics.name: Linear transformations and standard matrices
know: The definition T(u + v) = T(u) + T(v) and T(cu) = cT(u), and its consequences: T(0) = 0 and T keeps linear combinations
Domain, codomain and range; b is in the range of T(x) = Ax exactly when Ax = b is consistent
The standard matrix A = [T(e1) ... T(en)]: its columns are the images of the standard basis vectors
The rotation matrix [cos t, -sin t; sin t, cos t] and the reflections in the axes and in the lines y = x and y = -x
The matrix of first S, then T is the product (matrix of T)(matrix of S)
do: Find the standard matrix of a rotation followed by a reflection in R^2, or the other way round
Find the parameter for which a given vector lies in the range of T
Use the images of two vectors to find the standard matrix or the image of a third vector
Show that a map is not linear, for example because T(0) is not 0
pitfalls: Multiplying the matrices in the order the maps are named: the map applied first stands on the right
Taking T(0) = 0 as proof of linearity: it is necessary but not sufficient, as one of the Lecture 4 true/false slides shows
Using the counter-clockwise rotation matrix for a clockwise rotation: use minus the angle

topics.name: Matrix algebra and inverses
know: Sum, scalar multiple, transpose and the product AB by the column rule and the row-column rule, and when a product is defined
What fails for matrices: AB = BA, cancelling (AB = AC does not give B = C), and AB = 0 does not force A = 0 or B = 0
The inverse of a 2 x 2 matrix through ad - bc, and row reducing [A I] to [I A^-1] for larger matrices
The Invertible Matrix Theorem: for a square A, invertible equals n pivots, independent columns, columns spanning R^n, only the trivial solution of Ax = 0, Ax = b solvable for every b
do: Solve a matrix equation such as (XB^-1)^T = C for X and simplify to a product of A, B, C, their inverses and transposes
Compute a 3 x 3 inverse by row reduction, or the matrix X with AX = D for a diagonal D
Simplify a high power using a given relation such as A^3 = 3A
Refute an identity from ordinary algebra, such as (A + B)(A - B) = A^2 - B^2, with explicit 2 x 2 matrices
pitfalls: Losing the order when inverting or transposing a product: (AB)^-1 is B^-1 A^-1, not A^-1 B^-1
Using rules for numbers that fail for matrices, the point of the Warning slide in Lecture 5; the 2024 endterm asked exactly for a counterexample to such an expansion

topics.name: Subspaces, bases, dimension and rank
know: The subspace test: contains 0, closed under sums and scalar multiples; a line not through the origin or the set of unit vectors is not a subspace
Col A and Nul A; a basis of Col A is formed by the pivot columns of A itself, a basis of Nul A comes from the parametric vector form of Ax = 0
A basis is an independent spanning set, and a subspace has many bases
Coordinates [x]_B relative to a basis B, and back from [x]_B to x
Dimension, rank A = dim Col A, and the Rank Theorem: rank A + dim Nul A = number of columns
The Basis Theorem: in a p-dimensional subspace, p independent vectors, or p vectors that span, form a basis
do: Find bases of Col A and Nul A, or of a subspace given by one equation such as 3x2 + 2x3 + 3x4 = 0
Say which sets of columns of A are guaranteed to be a basis of Col A, given only an echelon form
Compute [x]_B, or write DNE when x is not in the span of B
Find the parameter for which dim Nul A takes a given value, and use the Rank Theorem on a matrix of given size
pitfalls: Taking the pivot columns of the echelon form instead of the matching columns of A (the warning slide in Lecture 8; Endterm 2024 question 3 tests it)
Assuming Nul A and Col A can never be equal: for a 2 x 2 matrix of rank 1 they can (Resit 2022)

topics.name: Determinants
know: Cofactor expansion along any row or column, with the checkerboard of signs; the determinant of a triangular matrix is the product of its diagonal
Row operations: a replacement keeps det, a swap changes its sign, scaling a row by k multiplies it by k; the same holds for columns
det(AB) = det(A) det(B), det(A^T) = det(A), det(A^-1) = 1/det(A), and det(cA) = c^n det(A) for an n x n matrix
A is invertible exactly when det(A) is not 0
do: Compute a 4 x 4 or 5 x 5 determinant by expanding along rows and columns with many zeros
Find the determinant of a matrix with permuted, scaled or combined rows or columns from the determinant of the original
Find all possible values of det(A) from a matrix equation such as A^2 = I
Find the parameter for which a matrix is singular
pitfalls: Writing det(cA) = c det(A) instead of c^n det(A); the midterm questions on det(-3B) and det(-2A) test exactly this
Losing a sign: each swap of two rows or columns flips it, so a cyclic shift of three columns keeps it

topics.name: Eigenvalues and diagonalisation
know: Av = lambda v with v not 0; the eigenspace of lambda is Nul(A - lambda I)
The characteristic equation det(A - lambda I) = 0 and algebraic multiplicity; a triangular matrix has its diagonal entries as eigenvalues
0 is an eigenvalue exactly when A is not invertible; eigenvectors for distinct eigenvalues are independent
Similar matrices, A = PBP^-1, share the characteristic polynomial and so the eigenvalues
A = PDP^-1 exists exactly when A has n independent eigenvectors, so when every geometric multiplicity equals the algebraic one; n distinct eigenvalues are enough
Powers through a diagonalisation: A^k = P D^k P^-1
do: Compute the eigenvalues and a basis of each eigenspace of a 2 x 2 or 3 x 3 matrix
Find the parameter for which a matrix with a repeated eigenvalue is diagonalisable
Read the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of A = PCP^-1 from C and P
Compute A^10, or one column of it, through a diagonalisation
Decide true or false for statements about the eigenvalues of A^T, A^2, AB or a row-equivalent matrix
pitfalls: Assuming a matrix is diagonalisable because its eigenvalues are real: a double eigenvalue also needs a two-dimensional eigenspace (Endterm 2023 question 4)
Believing row operations keep eigenvalues or diagonalisability; Resit 2023 asked for a counterexample
Giving eigenvectors of C as eigenvectors of A = PCP^-1: multiply them by P first (Endterm 2024 question 7)

topics.name: Complex eigenvalues and dynamical systems
know: Complex eigenvalues of a real matrix come in conjugate pairs, with conjugate eigenvectors
For a real 2 x 2 matrix with eigenvalue a - bi (b not 0) and eigenvector v: A = PCP^-1 with P = [Re v, Im v] and C = [a, -b; b, a], a rotation combined with a scaling by r = sqrt(a^2 + b^2)
For diagonalisable A the system x_(k+1) = A x_k has general solution x_k = c1 lambda1^k v1 + ... + cn lambdan^k vn
The origin is an attractor if every |lambda| < 1, a repeller if every |lambda| > 1, a saddle point if there are some of each; an eigenvalue with |lambda| = 1 makes it none of these
With complex eigenvalues the trajectories spiral inwards when r < 1, outwards when r > 1, and stay on an ellipse when r = 1
do: Find a real P and C = [a, -b; b, a] with A = PCP^-1
Solve an initial value problem x_(k+1) = A x_k and give a formula for one coordinate
Classify the origin for given eigenvalues, also when one depends on a parameter
Find the smallest k with A^k = I for a matrix similar to a rotation
pitfalls: Combining C built from a - bi with the eigenvector of a + bi: the 2024 endterm solutions list that P as incorrect
Calling the origin an attractor when one eigenvalue equals 1 (Resit 2023 question 8)

topics.name: Orthogonality, projections and Gram-Schmidt
know: Inner product, length, distance and unit vectors; u and v are orthogonal when u . v = 0
The orthogonal complement W^perp, with (Row A)^perp = Nul A, (Col A)^perp = Nul A^T and dim W + dim W^perp = n
Orthogonal and orthonormal bases; coordinates relative to an orthogonal basis are c_i = (y . u_i)/(u_i . u_i)
U has orthonormal columns exactly when U^T U = I; a square such U is an orthogonal matrix, with inverse U^T
Projection onto a line and onto W given an orthogonal basis; y = y-hat + z with y-hat in W and z in W^perp, and y-hat is the point of W closest to y
The projection matrix P = U U^T for an orthonormal basis in the columns of U; P^2 = P, so its eigenvalues are 0 and 1
The Gram-Schmidt process, which turns any basis of a subspace into an orthogonal one
do: Find a basis of W^perp by solving a homogeneous system
Compute a projection, the distance from a vector to a subspace, or one row or column of the projection matrix
Run Gram-Schmidt on two or three vectors in R^3 or R^4
Prove short statements such as: if ||u - v|| = ||u + v||, then u and v are orthogonal
pitfalls: Using the projection formula with a basis that is not orthogonal: run Gram-Schmidt first, as Endterm 2024 question 5 requires
Forgetting that Gram-Schmidt gives a zero vector when an input vector depends on the earlier ones (a Lecture 18 polling question)

topics.name: Least-squares problems
know: A least-squares solution x-hat minimises ||b - Ax||, and x-hat is one exactly when A x-hat is the projection of b onto Col A
The normal equations A^T A x = A^T b; the solution is unique exactly when the columns of A are independent, so when A^T A is invertible
The least-squares error ||b - A x-hat||
Linear models: design matrix X, parameter vector beta and observation vector y, for the line y = beta0 + beta1 x and for other curves such as a parabola
Residuals: the vertical differences between the data and the fitted curve
do: Find all least-squares solutions, including a whole line of them when the columns of A are dependent
Compute the least-squares error
Fit the least-squares line through four data points by hand
Set up the design matrix for another model curve
pitfalls: Giving the squared error instead of the error: Resit 2023 gave 1 of 3 points for 38 instead of sqrt(38)
Assuming the least-squares solution is unique when the columns of A are dependent

topics.name: Symmetric matrices
know: A real symmetric matrix (A^T = A) has real eigenvalues, and eigenvectors for different eigenvalues are orthogonal
Orthogonally diagonalisable means A = PDP^T with P an orthogonal matrix
The spectral theorem: a real matrix is orthogonally diagonalisable exactly when it is symmetric
The method: eigenvalues, a basis of each eigenspace, Gram-Schmidt inside each eigenspace, then normalise
do: Find an orthogonal eigenvector basis of R^3 for a symmetric matrix with a two-dimensional eigenspace
Find the parameter for which a given PDP^-1 is symmetric
Refute statements such as: a matrix similar to a symmetric matrix is orthogonally diagonalisable
pitfalls: Leaving the columns of P orthogonal but not of length 1 (the remark in Lecture 20)
Skipping Gram-Schmidt inside a two-dimensional eigenspace: only vectors from different eigenspaces are orthogonal automatically

prerequisites: Secondary-school algebra: solving equations, fractions and simplifying expressions by hand, as no calculator is allowed
Exact sine and cosine values of standard angles such as 30, 45, 60 and 120 degrees, for rotation matrices
Complex numbers: arithmetic, conjugates, modulus and argument, for Lectures 13 and 14
Vectors in the plane and in space, and lines and planes in parametric form
Basic logic: if-then statements, proof by contradiction and counterexamples
practical: No lab or project counts towards the grade. Each lecture has a pre-lecture video and exercises and post-lecture exercises, many in Grasple. Each week also has construction blocks and one instruction (exercise) session; the 2024-25 instruction exercises are in the archive. For Lectures 7 and 17 there are academic reasoning tests in Grasple with four true/false statements, where teachers give feedback on uploaded proofs.
studyAdvice: Linear systems, matrix algebra and subspaces with rank together carry about 41 percent of the points and appear on every paper; make row reduction, inverses and bases routine first.
Take the midterm: it covers Lectures 1 to 10 in short-answer questions, can only raise your final grade, and is your best check on the first half.
Determinants take 4 percent of the slides but about 10 percent of the points, on every paper. Drill expansion along sparse rows and the rules for det(cA), det(A^T), det(A^-1) and row swaps.
From Lecture 11 on, keep up week by week: eigenvalues feed diagonalisation, dynamical systems and symmetric matrices, and about 60 percent of the endterm and resit points come from Lectures 11 to 20.

Practise academic reasoning with the Recall, Try, Answer strategy from Lectures 7 and 17: write down the definitions, decide true or false, then give a full proof or an explicit numerical counterexample.
Do the archive papers without a calculator; several questions return with new numbers, such as the projection matrix for the same two vectors in Resit 2022 and Resit 2023.
Learn the Invertible Matrix Theorem as one connected list and add determinant and eigenvalue conditions as you meet them: multiple-choice and true/false questions lean on it.
